This device is intended to assist physicians, particularly non-dermatologists, in evaluating suspicious skin lesions to aid referral decisions, but it is not a standalone diagnostic tool.

To evaluate skin lesions suggestive of melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and/or squamous cell carcinoma in patients aged 40 and above to assist in the decision regarding referral to a dermatologist. It is used to assist in evaluating suspicious skin lesions in clinical settings, not as a screening tool or standalone diagnostic. Elastic Scattering Spectroscopy (ESS) spectral recordings from intact primary skin lesions suspected of melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, or squamous cell carcinoma, in patients aged 40 and above. Lesions should not be previously biopsied, recurrent, metastatic, on scars, tattoos, sunburned skin, hairy areas, palms, soles, mucosal surfaces, genitals, ears, within 1 cm of the eye, or under nails. The device provides results as "Monitor" for a negative result or "Investigate Further" for a positive result, based on analysis of backscattered light spectra by a proprietary ML-derived classifier algorithm. For "Investigate Further" results, a Similarity Score of 1-10 is displayed, indicating greater similarity to malignant lesions seen in training data. The device is an adjunctive, software-aided diagnostic tool intended to assist physicians, particularly those not trained in dermatology, in evaluating suspicious skin lesions and making referral decisions. It is not a standalone diagnostic and does not replace biopsy, pathology, or physician judgment. Physicians and trained healthcare professionals in clinical settings, including primary care physicians, especially those not trained in the clinical diagnosis and management of skin cancer. Performance has not been specifically evaluated in patients with increased risk for skin cancer (e.g., inherited/drug-induced photosensitivity, genetic predisposition, immune compromise). Artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) based software algorithm utilizing Elastic Scattering Spectroscopy (ESS). The final architecture has 10 neural networks trained on different architectures and training set variations, including feedforward neural networks and deep neural networks based on ResNet-18 architecture. The device was trained on an expansive databank of spectral scans of over 2000 lesions from multiple health care settings, comprising over 10,000 readings. The training dataset contained 950 lesions (approximately 4,200 spectra) and included a majority of older patients (age 60-79), Fitzpatrick phototypes I-III, and individuals who self-identified as White. Lesions on the head and neck constituted the majority of the training data. The dataset included BCC, SCC, melanoma (including severely atypical nevi), and various benign lesion mimics. The DermaSensor device utilizes optical spectroscopy and an AI/ML-based software algorithm. Algorithm development involved initial work on ESS technology to identify optimal wavelength range and spectral features. Clinical development included blinded, multicenter clinical studies. A prospective, multicenter clinical validation study was conducted at 4 US investigational sites, enrolling 614 lesions from 394 participants. The device was validated against histopathologic evaluation by expert dermatologists. [Publication](https://www.bu.edu/bmo/files/2024/02/Dermasensor-paper-2.pdf) NCT05126173 — The device was evaluated in the DERM-SUCCESS study, an observational study led by the Mayo Clinic across 22 study centers, enrolling over 1000 patients. A companion clinical utility study also investigated DermaSensor’s usage with 108 physicians.

In a clinical validation study, the overall device sensitivity was 97.04% and specificity was 26.22%. No statistically significant difference was found between the device and dermatologist sensitivity (P = .8203). The overall Negative Predictive Value (NPV) was 89.58% and Positive Predictive Value (PPV) was 57.54%. DermaSensor is a handheld, FDA-cleared point-of-care device that uses elastic scattering spectroscopy (ESS) and a proprietary machine learning algorithm to assess skin lesions suspicious for melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma. It takes five non-invasive spectral recordings from a lesion and outputs an objective result to support non-dermatologist physicians' referral decisions.

Evaluate skin lesions suggestive of melanoma, BCC, and/or SCC in patients aged 40 and above to assist in referral decisions; used alongside clinical assessment by physicians who are not dermatologists; not a screening tool and not for sole diagnostic use. Applied non-invasively to an intact skin lesion already assessed as suspicious for skin cancer; takes five short (~30 microsecond) broadband light spectral recordings (300-900nm) analyzed by an onboard microspectrometer. An objective 'Investigate Further' (positive) or 'Monitor' (negative) result; positive results include a Similarity Score from 1-10 indicating similarity to malignant lesions, generated by a proprietary neural network trained on over 2,000 histopathologically confirmed lesions. Adjunctive referral support only, used alongside clinical assessment (including visual analysis) by physicians who are not dermatologists; does not replace clinician judgment, biopsy, or definitive diagnosis, and is not the sole diagnostic criterion. Physicians who are not dermatologists (e.g. primary care, family medicine, internal medicine, walk-in clinics). No certification is required, but the physician must perform a clinical assessment including visual lesion analysis prior to use; Instructions for Use and supplemental training materials are provided. Patients aged 40 and above with skin lesions already assessed as suspicious for skin cancer.

False positives/negatives may lead to unnecessary referrals or missed malignant lesions. The DERM-SUCCESS study found overall device sensitivity of 95.5% (lower bound 91.7%); when used to aid PCP referral decisions, device use decreased PCPs' false negative rate from 18.0% to 8.6%. Training data bias due to proprietary, non-public datasets; DERM-ASSESS III was a company-sponsored study; lack of independent, non-company-funded validation.

Validated across three prospective clinical studies: DERM-SUCCESS Validation, DERM-ASSESS III, and DERM-SUCCESS Clinical Utility. [Publication](https://www.dermasensor.com/wp-content/uploads/Clinical-Evidence-Three-Studies.pdf) DERM-SUCCESS Prospective Skin Cancer Validation Study; DERM-ASSESS III Prospective Melanoma Validation Study; DERM-SUCCESS Prospective Clinical Utility Study.

Device sensitivity of 95.5% (DERM-SUCCESS) was superior to study PCP investigators (83.0%); AUROC 0.803 vs 0.736 for PCPs. DERM-ASSESS III showed AUROC 0.758, comparable to dermatologists (0.747). Subgroup performance was similar across Fitzpatrick skin type groups. 95.5% (DERM-SUCCESS) 0.803 (DERM-SUCCESS) 20.7% (DERM-SUCCESS)

In a DERM-SUCCESS sub-analysis of 1,005 patients, 72% were Fitzpatrick I-III and 28% were Fitzpatrick IV-VI; device sensitivity (96% vs 92%) and AUROC (0.779 vs 0.764) were similar between the two groups. However, the pivotal trial population was 97.1% White and only 13% were the most pigmented skin types (Fitzpatrick V/VI); full training dataset demographics are not publicly disclosed, and the FDA has required post-market performance testing in underrepresented populations.

Algorithm is locked per FDA requirements and not continually updated; revalidated and updated approximately every two years, requiring FDA resubmission and clearance each time. DERM analyzes dermoscopic images of skin lesions using AI-based algorithms. It returns a suspected diagnosis and referral recommendation to help screen, triage, and assess patients for skin cancer. This helps conserve dermatologist capacity by triaging non-cancerous lesions away from urgent pathways.

DERM is an AI-based skin lesion analysis device intended for the screening, triage, and assessment of skin lesions suspicious for skin cancer, aiming to improve access to assessments and conserve dermatologist capacity. DERM achieved AUROC of 91.8-95.8% for melanoma detection across camera devices, with 99.8% negative predictive value (vs. 98.9% for dermatologists); AUROC 0.85-0.89 for SCC and 0.87-0.89 for BCC. In real-world deployment across 170,000+ patients, DERM demonstrated 97% pathway sensitivity for malignant melanoma, exceeding the 95% target, with no adverse safety events or missed high-risk cancers reported. Subgroup performance across Fitzpatrick skin types I-VI showed no meaningful difference in detection quality. 91.8-95.8% 99.8% 97% (real-world deployment, 170,000+ patients)

Primarily evaluated on Fitzpatrick skin types I-IV; should be used with caution on other skin types. Real-world deployment data across 170,000 patients (all Fitzpatrick types I-VI) showed darker skin types underrepresented relative to their population share, though DERM correctly identified all melanomas, SCCs, and BCCs in Fitzpatrick V/VI patients since 2020, and subgroup analysis found no difference in performance quality for darker skin tones. However, darker skin types remain underrepresented in the training dataset (only 2.2% Fitzpatrick IV-VI in the DERM-003 study), limiting generalizability, and DERM cannot currently assess palmoplantar/subungual lesions, which disproportionately affect darker-skinned patients.

SkinVision is an AI-powered mobile app that lets users photograph moles and skin lesions with a smartphone and receive a low/medium/high risk indication to support preventive self-monitoring and decisions about seeking a dermatologist. It combines a clinically validated convolutional neural network algorithm with dermatologist-reviewed training images, and is not intended to provide a diagnosis.

Analyze smartphone photos of skin lesions and classify them with a low/medium/high risk indication to empower self-monitoring and inform decisions about seeking a medical follow-up; not intended as a diagnostic tool. A smartphone photo of a skin lesion captured via the app's guided camera (lesion centered, in focus, area around the mole clear); users can also complete an in-app questionnaire for skin type and risk-factor assessment. A categorical risk indication (low/medium/high) per lesion plus a triage recommendation, generated by a proprietary convolutional neural network trained on dermatologist-reviewed smartphone images; not a diagnostic report. Presented as risk categories with educational explanations to support preventive self-monitoring, not a diagnostic report; a high-risk result prompts a recommendation to seek professional evaluation but does not itself confirm skin cancer. Individuals at risk of developing skin cancer (consumer/self-use), as well as healthcare professionals who may use the output as supplementary information; no clinical knowledge or expertise is required, only a smartphone and the app. General consumers seeking to self-monitor skin lesions for skin cancer risk; not intended for persons under age 18.

Independent studies report sensitivity/specificity varying by evaluation, e.g. 73% sensitivity/83% specificity for melanoma in one study and 95.1% sensitivity/78.3% specificity for (pre)malignant conditions in another; roughly 45% of lesions in one study could not be analyzed by the app; agreement between the app and dermatologists was limited in some evaluations. Sensitivity/specificity estimates vary substantially across studies and between company and independent evaluations; the proprietary training dataset's demographic composition (including skin tone representation) is not publicly disclosed, limiting evaluation of generalizability and equity.

Proprietary convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture for smartphone image-based skin lesion risk assessment. Trained and validated on a proprietary dataset of dermatologist-reviewed smartphone images; one published validation used 131,873 images from 31,449 users (Jan 2016-Aug 2018) rated for risk by dermatologists. Full dataset composition and demographic breakdown are not publicly disclosed. Clinically validated per ISO 14971 risk management and ISO 13485/27001 quality and security standards; reviewed by an independent team of EU-appointed medical technology experts. [Publication](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31494983/) Not disclosed

Reported sensitivity ranges from approximately 73% to over 95% across different independent studies, with specificity varying accordingly (78-83%); company-reported figures tend to be higher than third-party evaluations. The company's research pipeline lists 'performance across diverse skin types and demographics' as an ongoing area of work.

Algorithm is continuously updated using newly submitted user images; user data is retained up to 12 months after account deletion.
